title: Every Spark Liquidity Layer venue is specified by a uniform Instance Configuration Document, so onboarding a venue is a template fill rather than a prose amendment
content:
Each venue in the Spark Liquidity Layer gets its own Instance Configuration Document with an invariant internal shape. Comparing the SparkLend Dai (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.1.3), USDT (.1.4), pyUSD (.1.5), wETH (.1.6) and Aave Prime USDS (.2.1) documents, every one contains the same numbered slots: `Instance Identifiers` (Network, Target Protocol, Asset Supplied By Spark Liquidity Layer, Token), `Contract Addresses` (Token Address, Underlying Asset Address), `Rate Limit IDs`, `Rate Limits` (inflow and outflow sub-documents), `Off-chain Operational Parameters`, and a sibling `Instance-specific Operational Processes` document.

The structure is load-bearing for governance, not just tidiness. Because the schema is fixed, a governance change that adds a venue does not require drafting new normative language — it instantiates the template and populates leaf values. Diffing two instances is mechanical, and an omitted parameter is visible as an empty slot rather than as silence.

It also localises change. Adjusting a rate limit touches one leaf document at a stable Atlas address (e.g. A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.1.4.2.4.1 for USDT inflow), so the amendment surface is a single number rather than a paragraph whose meaning must be re-litigated.

The cost is that the template is only as expressive as its slots. Where a venue needs a parameter the schema does not anticipate — Aave's `Pool` field appears only in the Aave instances (.2.1.2.2.3) — the structure must be extended, and per-protocol divergence starts to leak into what is nominally a uniform format.
description: The fixed slots are network, target protocol, supplied asset, receipt token, contract addresses, RateLimitIDs, rate limits and off-chain parameters — identical across SparkLend and Aave instances.
